course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Reconstruction
lesson.summary: How Presidents Lincoln and Johnson and Congress disagreed over Reconstruction, what the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments did, how the women's rights movement split, and what Reconstruction achieved in the South.
learningGoals: Compare the Reconstruction plans of Lincoln, Johnson, and Congress.
Explain what the Reconstruction amendments did and how they divided the women's rights movement.
Explain the short-term successes of Reconstruction and the reasons that it ultimately failed.
lesson.bigIdea: Reconstruction changed the relationship between the states and the federal government and gave African Americans citizenship and the vote, but it failed to secure those rights because of Southern resistance and the North's waning resolve.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to use evidence from sources to support a claim. For this topic the main evidence is the text of the amendments and the actions of the president and Congress, so keep track of what each one did and what it left undone.

sections.title: Plans for Reconstruction

blocks.text: Reconstruction altered relationships between the states and the federal government and led to debates over new definitions of citizenship, particularly regarding the rights of African Americans, women, and other minorities. Leaders disagreed about how to bring the Southern states back even before the war ended. In 1863 Lincoln proposed the Ten Percent Plan, under which a state could form a new government when ten percent of its voters of 1860 swore loyalty to the Union and accepted the end of slavery. Radical Republicans in Congress, such as Thaddeus Stevens and Charles Sumner, thought the plan too lenient and wanted stronger protection for the freed people. Congress passed the Wade–Davis Bill in 1864, which required a majority of voters to take an oath, and Lincoln let it die by a pocket veto.

After Lincoln's assassination in April 1865, President Andrew Johnson, a Southern Democrat, pardoned most former Confederates and allowed the Southern states to form new governments quickly. Those governments passed Black Codes, which limited the freedom of formerly enslaved people, and elected former Confederate leaders to Congress. Congress refused to seat them. It created the Freedmen's Bureau to help the freed people, passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over Johnson's veto, and in 1867 passed the Reconstruction Acts, which divided most of the South into five military districts and required states to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment and to allow Black men to vote. In 1868 the House impeached Johnson, and the Senate fell one vote short of removing him.

sections.takeaway: Lincoln and Johnson favored a quick and lenient restoration, and Congress, led by the Radical Republicans, took control of Reconstruction in 1867.

sections.title: The Reconstruction amendments

blocks.text: The 13th Amendment abolished slavery, while the 14th and 15th amendments granted African Americans citizenship, equal protection under the laws, and voting rights. The 13th Amendment was ratified in 1865. The 14th Amendment (1868) made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens, which overturned the Dred Scott ruling, and barred the states from denying equal protection of the laws. The 15th Amendment (1870) barred the national government and the states from denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.

The women's rights movement was both emboldened and divided over the 14th and 15th amendments. Many women had worked for abolition and hoped that the vote would be extended to them. The 14th Amendment used the word “male” in the Constitution for the first time, and the 15th Amendment did not mention sex. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed the 15th Amendment because it left out women, and in 1869 they formed the National Woman Suffrage Association. Lucy Stone, Julia Ward Howe, and others supported the amendment, argued that the vote for Black men should not wait, and formed the American Woman Suffrage Association.

sections.takeaway: The amendments ended slavery and defined citizenship and voting rights for African American men, while women's suffrage leaders divided over them.

sections.title: Reconstruction in the South

blocks.text: Efforts by radical and moderate Republicans to change the balance of power between Congress and the presidency and to reorder race relations in the defeated South yielded some short-term successes. Reconstruction opened up political opportunities and other leadership roles to formerly enslaved persons. Black men voted and held office in Southern state governments and in Congress, and in 1870 Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first African American to serve in the Senate. Freed people founded their own churches and schools, and the new state governments set up public schools.

Reconstruction ultimately failed, due both to determined Southern resistance and the North's waning resolve. White Southerners who opposed Reconstruction used violence and intimidation. The Ku Klux Klan, founded in 1866, attacked Black voters and Republican officials, and Congress passed the Enforcement Acts in 1870 and 1871 to try to stop it. Many Northerners grew tired of the effort, and attention turned to economic problems after the Panic of 1873. Topic 5.11 follows the end of Reconstruction.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Opponents of Reconstruction claimed that Black officeholders were incompetent and the new governments corrupt. Historians point instead to the violence, resistance, and loss of Northern will that ended it.

sections.takeaway: Reconstruction brought real political gains for African Americans, but violence and the loss of Northern support undermined them.

connections.title: Why the gains did not last
connections.body: The amendments remained in the Constitution, but the practice of Reconstruction ended. Topic 5.11 explains why.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the promise of Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address, “with malice toward none,” compare with the policies of Congress after 1867?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that Lincoln stressed reconciliation and a lenient restoration, while Congress after 1867 imposed military rule and conditions that protected the rights of the freed people.
